$comment: Who says which words in this chapter (docs/voice-narration-plan.md section 3). Drafted by `npm run voice:script`; a line with no entry is read by the narrator. A person checks each draft and sets `reviewed` to true; re-drafting only touches missing and stale entries.

lines.text: A wagon wheel drops into a rut, and gem chips spill everywhere.
"WATCH YOUR BOOTS!"
booms the lead drover, who runs the river crossing. Help him catch the chips, or stand back and watch.
Your bigfoot looks once, and points. Under the wheel. In a hoofprint. Inside somebody's boot. Every chip goes back.
"Never seen eyes like that,"
the drover booms.
"I'll remember you folks."
At the west branch, the ford line is two days long. A faun named Burdock sells numbered pebbles and very expensive honeycakes. Your pebble says 412.
"My lucky number!"
he says. The ford is on number 9.
Three coins buy a honeycake the size of one coin.
"My lucky number,"
says Burdock, meaning your money. You save the cake for someone who needs it.
Burdock's goat, Pudding, gallops down the line with the pebble bucket on her head. Numbers fly everywhere.
"My bucket! My GOAT!"
wails Burdock. Chase her, or sort the spilled numbers for a honeycake.
Pudding gallops off with the bucket on her head. Every few steps she stops at a cabbage stall to chew.
"Wait for the chew!"
wails Burdock.
"Then grab!"
You ask people their numbers and sort the pebbles fairly. Burdock gives you a honeycake.
"This has never happened,"
he says.
"Tell nobody."
Pudding wanders back.
A kitsune named Tamsin Three-Cards shuffles cards on a barrel.
"Find the Sun Card! Win a front-of-the-line pebble!"
Her third tail twitches. Catch her trick, walk away, or help her fool the crowd.
You keep your coins. Tamsin tips her hat.
"Come back when you feel lucky."
Behind you, somebody loses again, very loudly.
A cheerful ladler named Wend gives away free soup under the dark-robed helpers' tent.
"Kindness first,"
says Wend. A little crystal on the ladle cord shivers whenever a gem wagon passes.
"Since the red night,"
says Wend, lifting the crystal.
"Means something, doesn't it?"
Another wagon passes. The crystal hums. Wend changes the subject to soup.
Wend beams and fills your bowls again.
"Kindness first."
The crystal shivers at another wagon.
A gang in red scarves pushes up the line.
"Ford closes tomorrow!"
their leader shouts. An old faun doubts it. Hold the line, and the scarves may treat you fairly later. Or fetch the drovers.
Your kitsune smiles the sweetest smile in the line.
"Haven't you heard? The back is the front now."
The red scarves sprint to the back. It takes them an hour to work it out.
Tamsin strolls up, shuffling.
"Find the Sun Card, win a place at the front!"
The red scarves play for an hour and never find it. By then the line has rolled on without them.
A centaur relay-runner skids up.
"Message for the drovers! Can't stop!"
The note says RIVER RISING. CROSS SLOW. Run it, sing it down the line, or fly it to the ford.

You weave through wagons, goats and campfires, and slap the note into the lead drover's hand. He reads it, nods, and slows the crossing to a careful walk. When you get back, the runner tosses you a brave whistle.
"The relay remembers,"
she says.
Your griffin crosses the whole line in four wingbeats. The lead drover reads the note and nods. Back in line, the runner whistles.
"The relay could use a friend with wings."

Pick one job before dusk. Free a stuck wagon, and its crew will help you in the ford. Fix the marker line for an easier ford. Or help the Brackens, a faun family with a cracked wheel, and ride their cart.
"We are being very brave,"
says Littlest Bracken.
The marker line stands straight again, every post pointing the safe way to the ford. A relay-runner slows just long enough to say,
"The relay remembers."
At the big campfire, a troupe acts out the red night with blankets and saucepans. Their mountain gets the hiccups.
"New mountain, darlings!"
cries the leader. Play it, or tell them what you really heard.
The troupe leader hands you a red blanket and points at a barrel.
"Climb up, darling, and be a MOUNTAIN!"
You describe the hum in every gem. The leader changes the play. Now the mountain is quiet, and the falling stones sing.
"Much spookier,"
she whispers.
Your kitsune changes the play on the spot. In the new ending, the stones are not treasure. They are a puzzle. The crowd likes it better.
"Annoyingly better,"
mutters the leader.
At a remedy stall, bell charms ring whenever a gem wagon passes. The witch, Mother Thrum, winces over her glasses.
"What do you actually want?"
she asks.
Mother Thrum hands over a sunbloom potion.
"Feet next. Listen first."
Another wagon makes every charm ring. She closes her eyes and counts to three.
Mother Thrum gives you a tuned bell charm. Near any gem, it sings the same ancient note.
"Older than the road,"
she says. On her shelf, a stone rings inside a wool sock.
You leave the ringing stone in its sock. Mother Thrum tucks it behind the counter.
"Some questions take longer."
You head back to camp with the tuned charm.
You tell her where it fell from, and that you will take it back. The ringing stops the moment the stone touches your dragonling's hands.
"There,"
says Mother Thrum softly.
"It knows. Keep it warm."
Mother Thrum listens all the way to the end, then hands you the sock with the stone in it.
"That's the Ford Stone. Take it somewhere it stops ringing,"
she says.
"I'd like some sleep."
You say something about gems and glory, and Mother Thrum's charms all go quiet at once, which feels like an answer.
"Not yet,"
she says kindly.
"Ask yourself again at the mountain."
At dawn the lead drover sings the crossing verse: slow, slow, wait, slow.
"My ford, my pace,"
he booms. The river is higher. Learn the verse, or study the water.
The lead drover sings it again, thumping one step for each line: slow, and slow, and wait, and slow.
"Now sing it back,"
he booms.
"In order."
By the third time through, you are singing with him.
"Huh,"
he booms.
"You've got it."
The verse sits in your chest like a drum.
The river is wide and fast.
"One wagon at a time,"
booms the lead drover. The jobs you did in the line can help now. How will you cross?
"HEY, RED SCARVES!"
you shout. Their leader shrugs.
"Fair's fair."
The whole gang wades in, and together you heave the wagon upright while the drakes squabble over bread.
Two young glassback crabs have parked on the first crossing stones. Wheels come close. Claws click. Wheels back away.
"Back to the reeds, please,"
booms the lead drover. The crabs ignore him.
The crabs shuffle back to the reeds like small dukes leaving a party. The drover gives you a river charm.
"Polite neighbors,"
he booms, and begins his verse.
Clink, clink, clink. The bowls stack up neat as a tower, and Wend slips a honeycake into your pocket.
"Kindness first,"
he says.
One bowl lands in the mud, then three. Wend laughs, wipes them off and ladles you a bowl anyway.
"Kindness first,"
he says. No honeycake, though.
Up goes the awning, and the runner thunders through without a scrape. She flips you two coins over her shoulder.
"Thanks, line!"
The awning sags just as she passes, and she ducks, skids and bounces off a water barrel.
"Rude!"
she calls, and does not tip.
The stuck wagon leans hard into its rut. Tap when the marker crosses the gold to give it one good heave. The drover has named the rut.
"Do not encourage it."
